raw_response.country: Developing countries (global/multi-region overview; illustrative secondary tables cite India, Kenya, Republic of Korea, Colombia, Cyprus, Egypt, Ghana, Haiti, Uruguay, Democratic Republic of Yemen, and Zaire)

criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban and rural drinking water supply and sanitation coverage and service provision challenges across developing countries during the UN International Drinking Water Supply and Sanitation Decade.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, yes: the paper discusses institutional frameworks, utility autonomy, decentralization, private/cooperative participation, and tariff/cost-recovery policies. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it is borderline/unclear: while it conceptually discusses tariff/cost-recovery rules (long-run marginal cost pricing and lifeline subsidies) and utility ownership/regulatory structure options, much of the paper addresses macro-level Integrated Water Resource Planning (IWRP), general sector management, and project financing options rather than empirically analysing a concrete rule-type mechanism governing household access. Regardless of Criterion 2 reading, the paper is excluded for lack of empirical evidence (Criterion 3).
criterion_notes.c3: No primary empirical evidence, empirical study design, or systematic empirical synthesis. The article is a narrative policy overview and conceptual framework paper (proposing Integrated Water Resource Planning and general economic/institutional principles) accompanied only by illustrative secondary summary tables reproduced from WHO and World Bank reports. Excluded under E05.
criterion_notes.c4: Reproduces secondary aggregate WHO regional water and sanitation coverage tables (1970-1990) and a secondary four-country table on subsidized rural water connections by income group (from Briscoe and deFerranti 1988), but conducts no empirical outcome evaluation.
criterion_notes.c5: Because this is a non-empirical policy and conceptual overview, there is no identifiable empirical study design, analytical sample, or tested exposure-outcome relationship.

evidence_quotes.quote: Governments were urged to provide all their citizens with clean water and adequate sanitation by 1990.
Tables 1-4 present information, for both water supply and sanitation coverage, by region, from 1970 to 1990. Because of data constraints, these numbers are merely indicative estimates.

Setting the price of water supply and sewerage services strictly equal to marginal costs, at the market clearing point (where supply equals demand), is economically efficient because it helps to maximize the net benefits of water use.
A complete analysis of the effectiveness or suitability of various water supply organizations would be a major task in itself, and is outside the scope of this paper.

Better management, staff accountability, options for decentralization and private participation and innovative financing methods were also discussed as methods to help improve water utility performance.

raw_response.rationale: Full text read (16 pages; published as 'Water supply policies and issues in developing countries' by Mohan Munasinghe in Natural Resources Forum, Feb 1990, matching the record metadata with minor bibliographic title/year variation). Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Although the paper discusses developing-country water and sanitation access alongside tariff/cost-recovery concepts, institutional organization, and Integrated Water Resource Planning (IWRP), it is a narrative policy overview and conceptual planning essay that relies solely on illustrative secondary summary tables from WHO and World Bank reports, with no primary data, no empirical methodology, and no systematic empirical synthesis. It would likewise be excluded under the plain wording of Criterion 2 because Criterion 3 is not met.
raw_response.study_design: Policy overview and conceptual planning framework (non-empirical)
